## What you will do

In about 30 minutes you will **look inside** a public collection of 7.5 million crop photographs, **download 10 of them**, and **open them in R** with the same tools we used in the practical. You do not need an account, a password or any special software: R is enough.

::: {.callout-note}
**Work in pairs and download only a few photos.** The collection is huge and we share the wifi of the room. Ten photos per pair are enough. Never try to download a whole folder.
:::

## 1. What is this collection?

**Artemis and Image Safari** are crop image datasets of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, stored on Amazon Web Services as open data.

| | Artemis | Image Safari |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Photographs | 1,387,663 | 6,081,555 |
| Crops | common bean, cowpea, soybean, sorghum | 18 crops |
| Countries | 4 | 9 (sub-Saharan Africa) |
| Extra information | agronomic, genotypic and environmental metadata linked to the photos | one JSON metadata file per image |

- 40,558 photographs have **annotations** of plant organs (segmentation, detection, points, scribbles): 10,887 in Artemis and 29,671 in Image Safari.
- It is **not** a plant disease dataset: the annotations describe crops and plant organs. Disease detection is only a possible use.
- Photographs are JPEG files at the original size of the camera. New images are added about once a year.
- **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0. You may use and share them if you give credit and keep the same licence.
- Two storage "buckets" in the region `us-west-2`; the name used here is `alliance-artemis-imagesafari`, with two main folders, `Artemis/` and `ImageSafari/`.

Source: [registry.opendata.aws/artemis-image-safari](https://registry.opendata.aws/artemis-image-safari/).

## 2. Set up (2 minutes)

```{r}
# xml2 reads the list of files; pliman we already have from the practical
if (!requireNamespace("xml2", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("xml2")
library(xml2)
library(pliman)
```

Now copy these two small functions. The first **lists** one folder of the collection, the second **downloads** one file.

```{r}
base <- "https://alliance-artemis-imagesafari.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com"

# List one "folder": returns the sub-folders and the files (key and size in MB)
list_bucket <- function(prefix = "", max_keys = 200) {
  url <- paste0(base, "/?list-type=2&delimiter=%2F&max-keys=", max_keys,
                "&prefix=", utils::URLencode(prefix, reserved = TRUE))
  x <- xml2::read_xml(url)
  xml2::xml_ns_strip(x)
  list(
    folders = xml2::xml_text(xml2::xml_find_all(x, "//CommonPrefixes/Prefix")),
    files   = data.frame(
      key     = xml2::xml_text(xml2::xml_find_all(x, "//Contents/Key")),
      size_mb = round(as.numeric(xml2::xml_text(xml2::xml_find_all(x, "//Contents/Size"))) / 1e6, 2)
    )
  )
}

# Download one file by its key into a local folder
get_photo <- function(key, dest = "artemis_photos") {
  dir.create(dest, showWarnings = FALSE)
  out <- file.path(dest, basename(key))
  utils::download.file(paste0(base, "/", utils::URLencode(key)), out, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  out
}
```

## 3. Look inside before you download

A *key* is the full name of a file, such as `Artemis/folder/photo.jpg`. A *prefix* is the beginning of a key, like a folder.

```{r}
list_bucket("")$folders         # the top level: you should see Artemis/ and ImageSafari/
```

```{r}
top <- list_bucket("Artemis/")
top$folders                      # the sub-folders of Artemis
head(top$files)                  # files at this level, if any
```

**Go down one folder at a time.** Choose a folder from the list, put it in `prefix`, and list it again:

```{r}
prefix <- "Artemis/"             # change it: paste one of the folders you saw, for example the first
cur <- list_bucket(prefix)
cur$folders
head(cur$files, 10)
```

Repeat until you reach a folder that has files ending in `.jpg` or `.jpeg`. Look also for folders or files with the words *annotations*, *metadata* or *json*: they tell you what each photo contains.

::: {.callout-note}
**The tree is deep.** The photographs are usually 4 to 6 folders down (crop, images, site, project, date, and so on). Do not go down by hand: this loop enters the first folder at each level until it finds files.

```{r}
prefix <- "Artemis/common-bean/images/ciat-arusha/disease-scouting/"   # any folder you chose
repeat {
  cur <- list_bucket(prefix)
  if (nrow(cur$files) > 0 || length(cur$folders) == 0) break
  prefix <- cur$folders[1]
}
prefix                            # the folder where the photographs are
head(cur$files, 10)
```

A real example that worked on the course: starting from the disease scouting folder of CIAT Arusha (Tanzania), the loop ends in `.../disease-scouting/2024--tza--feb/2024-02-02/unplotted/`, with photographs of about 4 MB each. Other sites in the common bean images are `ciat-kawanda`, `ciat-palmira`, `csu-fort-collins`, `naro-namulonge` and `tari-maruku`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
You can also read the same list in your **browser**: paste this address and add the folder after `prefix=`:

`https://alliance-artemis-imagesafari.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2&delimiter=/&prefix=Artemis/`

You will see an XML page. The names between `<Prefix>` are folders and the names between `<Key>` are files.
:::

**Write down** what you found: the path of the folder with photographs, the crop, and what metadata exists.

## 4. Download 10 photographs

```{r}
# 'cur' is the folder with photographs that you found in step 3
photos <- subset(cur$files, grepl("\\.jpe?g$", key, ignore.case = TRUE) & size_mb < 6)
nrow(photos)                      # how many photographs are in this folder?
sel <- head(photos$key, 10)       # the first 10 (you can choose others)
paths <- vapply(sel, get_photo, character(1))
paths
```

If a download fails with an error, try the next photograph: some keys may have special characters or the connection may be slow. Check the folder `artemis_photos/` in your project.

## 5. Look at the photographs in R

```{r}
img <- image_import(paths[1])      # pliman reads the file
dim(img)                           # height, width, colour channels
plot(img)
```

Now use the colour indices of the practical on a real field photograph:

```{r}
image_index(img, index = c("R", "GLI", "NGRDI"), ncol = 3, nrow = 1)
```

**Questions to discuss with your neighbour:**

1. Is the background uniform? Is the light even? Compare with the sample images of `pliman`.
2. Could you separate the plant from the soil with these indices? Which index works best?
3. What would you need to change in the way the photograph is taken to measure a trait reliably (see the pitfalls slide)?

## 6. Optional: the AWS command line

If you prefer a terminal, install the *AWS CLI* and use `--no-sign-request` (no account is needed):

```bash
aws s3 ls --no-sign-request s3://alliance-artemis-imagesafari/Artemis/
aws s3 cp --no-sign-request s3://alliance-artemis-imagesafari/Artemis/<folder>/<photo>.jpg .
```

## 7. If something fails

| Problem | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| `cannot open URL` or `403` | The network of the room may block Amazon. Try the browser address of step 3; if it also fails, use your phone as a hotspot, or ask the instructor for the sample folder |
| `could not find function "read_xml"` | Run `library(xml2)` |
| The list is empty | Check the `prefix`: it must end with `/` and match upper and lower case |
| Very slow | Download fewer photographs, or wait for your neighbour to finish |

## 8. Credit and good practice

- Cite the dataset with the **access date** and the address, and also the data descriptor: Mutuvi, S. et al. (2026), DOI [10.31220/agriRxiv.2026.00491](https://doi.org/10.31220/agriRxiv.2026.00491).
- Keep the licence (CC BY-SA 4.0) if you share the photographs or derived data.
- Keep the file names as they are: it is the safest way to link a photograph to its metadata and annotations later.

## About the project

Artemis was an initiative of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT with Mineral, supported by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (2022 to 2026). It piloted smartphone photography with artificial intelligence for breeding trials in Tanzania and Uganda; the project reports about 50% less phenotyping time and more than 1,000 plots per day, with an accuracy within 10% (r² above 0.8). This is the same idea of the practical: **a phone, a protocol and R**, scaled to a breeding programme.
